doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Hearing Ornette Coleman's quartet in New York
summary: She heard Coleman's quartet in a theater around 1959-60, was impressed but found it hard to understand, and later learned tunes like 'Lonely Woman' and 'Rambling'.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Yeah. Revlon and others that said that they would not sponsor his show, because of that reason. We see that shortsightedness has come to pass in recent years about that too . . . I just wanted . . . because that whole lineage came through there. What I’d like to do is now, having touched up on that, exciting things of Art Blakey or people like that . . . we mentioned Bobby and Horace. Let’s jump back up again to 1959, 1960, when another exciting quartet arrives in New York and makes quite a splash that carries over beyond the jazz circles to people like Gunther Schuller and Leonard Bernstein, that this is very innovative. We’re talking about the Ornette Coleman quartet.
I knew you were going to talk about Ornette. Yeah.
Did you hear that group in person? I know Milt Jackson told me they . . . many times the Modern Jazz Quartet would work opposite Ornette’s quartet.
Yeah, like at the Village Vanguard when Max [Gordon] used to have double bills there.
I heard Ornette. Not at the Vanguard. I’m trying to think. It was some theater. A theater that was temporarily . . .

Maybe the Jazz . . . No, not the Jazz Gallery. It doesn’t matter, because I remember being very impressed by the music. But here again, I was . . . I can’t remember who I went with. Here again it was one of those things where it seemed very hard for me to understand. He probably was playing some of his early things, like maybe “Lonely Woman” or something, which I’ve since learned to play. I do one or two of his things, like “Rambling.” I love to do that.
